t.3.46.1: As Sītā was speaking thus, Rāvaṇa, enraged, knitted a frown upon his brow and replied in harsh words.
t.3.46.2: O lady of fairest complexion, I am the half-brother of Vaiśravaṇa, his rival, the mighty ten-necked one named Rāvaṇa; may good fortune be yours.
t.3.46.3: He from fear of whom the devas, together with the Gandharvas, Piśācas, birds and serpents, flee in terror, just as creatures always flee from the fear of death.
t.3.46.5: Stricken with fear of me, Naravāhana abandoned his own prosperous seat and now dwells on Kailāsa, the best of mountains.
t.3.46.4: I am he by whom Vaiśravaṇa, my half-brother, was, for a certain reason, challenged in wrath to single combat, and by whom, attacking with valor, he was vanquished in battle.
t.3.46.6: I am he whose auspicious aerial chariot named Puṣpaka moves wherever one wishes, won by my valour, O fair lady, and by it I travel through the sky.
t.3.46.7: O Maithilī, at the mere sight of my face when anger has arisen in me, the gods with Śakra at their head flee in terror.
t.3.46.8: Wherever I stand, there the wind blows timidly, and out of fear the fierce-rayed sun becomes cool-rayed.
t.3.46.9: Wherever I stand and wherever I move, there the trees become still, their leaves unshaken, and the rivers' waters grow motionless.
t.3.46.10: On the far shore of the ocean is my beautiful city named Laṅkā, filled with fearsome Rākṣasas, like Indra's Amarāvatī.
t.3.46.11: Encircled by a white rampart and shining with splendor, the delightful city has courtyards of gold and gateways made of cat's-eye gems.
t.3.46.13: Living there with me, O Sītā, O princess, O high-minded one, you will no longer remember human women.
t.3.46.12: It is thronged with elephants, horses and chariots, resounding with the sound of musical instruments, and adorned with gardens crowded with trees whose fruits yield every desire.
t.3.46.15: Having installed his beloved son in his place, King Daśaratha then sent off to the forest his eldest son, who is of feeble valour.
t.3.46.14: Enjoying both human and divine pleasures, O fair-complexioned lady, you will no longer remember Rāma, a mere mortal whose life is spent.
t.3.46.16: O large-eyed lady, what will you do with that Rāma, who has fallen from his kingdom and lost his senses, a wretched ascetic?
t.3.46.17: You ought not to reject the lord of all the rākṣasas, who has come here himself out of desire, pierced by the arrows of Manmatha.
t.3.46.18: For having rejected me, you will come to fearful remorse, just as Urvaśī did after spurning Purūravas with her foot.
t.3.46.19: Thus addressed, Vaidehī, enraged, her eyes reddened, spoke harsh words to the lord of the rākṣasas in that lonely place.
t.3.46.20: How is it that, while proclaiming as your brother the god Vaiśravaṇa, who is revered by all beings, you wish to do something so wicked?
t.3.46.21: O Rāvaṇa, all the rākṣasas will surely perish, whose king you are, harsh, evil-minded and with your senses unconquered.
t.3.46.22: Having carried off Śacī, the wife of Indra, one might yet manage to live; but having taken me away, the wife of Rāma, there is no life for you.
t.3.46.23: One might live long after carrying off Śacī, whose beauty is beyond compare, from the very hand of the wielder of the thunderbolt; but having violated a woman such as me, O rākṣasa, there is no escape for you, even if you have drunk the nectar of immortality.
